IB 2027 · HL · Unit 4

Unit 4: Professional OOP Design

HL curriculum overview and structured learning plan.

Introduction

How do we build software that doesn't break?

This unit takes you from writing simple classes to designing Professional Systems. You will learn how to use Inheritance to reuse code, Polymorphism to create flexible logic, and Composition to build complex objects from smaller parts.

You'll start by mapping relationships (Is-A vs Has-A). Then you'll implement Inheritance Hierarchies and master Method Overriding to change behavior dynamically. Finally, you'll use Abstract Classes to define strict blueprints for your code.

Inheritance (Is-A)

Don't Repeat Yourself (DRY). Inheritance allows a child class to steal code from a parent.

  • Parent (Superclass): The generic version (e.g., Vehicle).
  • Child (Subclass): The specific version (e.g., Car). It gets all the variables and methods for free.
Polymorphism

Treating different objects the same way. The code adapts at runtime.

  • Overriding: A child class replaces a parent's method with its own version.
  • Dynamic Dispatch: The program decides which version to run while it is running.
Composition (Has-A)

Building complex objects by gluing simple ones together.

  • Composition: A Car has a Engine. If you destroy the Car, the Engine goes too.
  • Aggregation: A Library has a Book. If you close the Library, the Book still exists.
Abstraction

Hiding complex details behind a clean interface.

  • Abstract Class: A blueprint that cannot be created. It just defines what children MUST do.
  • Interfaces: Strictly defines a "contract" of methods.
Key Terminology
TermDefinition
Inheritance A mechanism where a new class derives attributes and methods from an existing class.
Polymorphism The ability of different classes to be treated as instances of the same general class through inheritance.
Method Overriding Providing a specific implementation of a method that is already provided by the parent class.
Abstract Class A class that cannot be instantiated and is used to define a common interface for subclasses.
Composition A 'part-of' relationship where the child object's lifecycle is dependent on the parent.
Aggregation A 'has-a' relationship where the child object can exist independently of the parent.
UML (Unified Modeling Language) A standard visual modeling language used to visualize, specify, construct, and document software systems.

  • Banking Systems (SavingsAccount extends Account)
